title: Position: AI Must Become Planet-Centered, Not Human-Centered
claim: Complex real-world problems have shared structural properties that cause AI systems to fail in systemic, unintended ways.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, tangled-yarn image, then property grid, then mechanism list
description: Three side-by-side panels read left to right. The left panel, titled 'Wicked problems', shows a tangle of multicolored yarn strands. Six colored yarn balls (red, purple, green, yellow, blue, black) sit around the edges and feed into the knot at the center. Italic text below defines wicked problems as complex, value-laden, ill-defined and interconnected, and says they appear in policy, technology and environment. The middle panel, on a pale yellow background, is titled 'Properties of wicked systems'. It lists eight terms in two columns, including Ambiguity, Non-stationarity, Emergence, Fragility, Trade-offs, Contestedness, Path-dependence, Coupling, Reflexivity and Uncertainty. The right panel, on a pink-mauve background, is titled 'Mechanisms for AI failure in wicked systems'. It has five bullets, each pairing a bolded failure cause with its consequence, such as 'Narrow framing of value → wrong objectives optimised'. The eye goes first to the colorful yarn tangle.
caption: Wicked problems, their structural sources of difficulty, and the mechanisms of AI failure.
abstract: This position paper argues that contemporary AI paradigms are insufficient for supporting complex global goals and introduces Planet-Centered AI (PCAI) as a design philosophy and research agenda that reorients AI toward planetary-scale socio-ecological systems and their long-term trajectories. A planet-centered approach is grounded in systems thinking, treating Earth as an interconnected whole of which humans are part. We diagnose recurring limitations across AI frameworks, many of which remain human-centered, and show why these become especially consequential under current planetary conditions characterized by systemic risk, non-stationarity, and deep uncertainty. We then articulate how PCAI reshapes the AI lifecycle, from problem formulation and model design to evaluation and deployment, by emphasizing alignment with global agendas, developing system-aware AI foundations, trajectory-oriented evaluation, and monitorability. Finally, we advance a falsifiable claim: AI systems optimized without explicit consideration of systemic consequences are more likely to exacerbate systemic instability than to mitigate it.
